questions.question: The diagram shows the view from above of two electromagnets. The direction of the currents is shown by arrows. Points X, Y and Z are in the plane of the two electromagnets. Which of the following is correct?
questions.answer: Stationary charges feel no magnetic force. The facing ends are like poles, so at Y there is no field component across the velocity. At X the field has a component perpendicular to the electron's velocity, giving a force out of the page.
options: A stationary electron at Z would experience a force to the right
A stationary proton at Z would experience a force to the right
An alpha particle moving to the right at Y would experience a force upwards out of the page
An electron moving to the right at X would experience a force upwards out of the page

questions.question: A block is placed on the edge of a horizontal turntable as shown. The turntable starts rotating from rest and speeds up. At some critical speed the block slides off the turntable. Which statement is true about this scenario?
questions.answer:
At the critical speed $\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\mu mg$, so $v=\sqrt{\mu gr}$, which does not depend on the mass.

*Note: the school's key gives B, rejecting C because the centripetal force depends on mass; but the maximum friction is also proportional to mass, so the mass cancels. B is loosely worded (the actual centripetal force can never exceed what friction supplies).*
options: The block slides when the centripetal force is less than friction
The block slides when the centripetal force is greater than friction
The critical speed is independent of the mass of the block
The critical speed is independent of the distance of the block from the centre

questions.question: A length of wire labelled ABC in a uniform magnetic field (into the page) is connected to an external circuit as shown. What is the direction of the force acting on the wire at point B?
questions.answer: The current flows from the positive terminal up through C and B towards A. By the right-hand rule, with the field into the page, the force at B is up and to the left (radially outwards).

questions.question: Which nuclear equation accurately shows the alpha decay of radium-223?
questions.answer: Alpha decay lowers the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

questions.question: A merry-go-round is shown. X is a point on the inner edge (radius 2 m) and Y is a point on the outer edge (radius 4 m). When it is spinning, which gives the correct ratios of (linear velocity of X : linear velocity of Y) and (angular velocity of X : angular velocity of Y)?
questions.answer: Both points have the same angular velocity, and $v=\omega r$.

questions.question: A very long train is travelling close to the speed of light. An observer on a platform watches the train travel past. Which of the following statements is true?
questions.answer: Time dilation is reciprocal: each observer measures the other's clocks running slow.
options: Time will appear to be running faster in the train according to the observer on the platform.
The platform will appear longer to the passenger on the train than to the observer on the platform.
A passenger on the train and the observer on the platform both measure time slowing in the other frame of reference.
The observer on the platform will observe a longer train while the observer on the train sees the platform shortened.

questions.question: A small positive sphere is projected into a region between two vertical charged plates as shown, in a vacuum. While the sphere remains in the uniform field, which statement is correct about the vertical component of its acceleration?
questions.answer: The electric force is horizontal, so the vertical acceleration is due to gravity alone.
options: greater than the acceleration due to gravity
less than the acceleration due to gravity
equal to the acceleration due to gravity
dependent on the size of the field

questions.question: A projectile is launched from the top of a cliff at point A and lands below at point D as shown. Ignoring air resistance, which of the following is correct?
questions.answer: A and C are at the same height, so by conservation of energy the speeds are equal.
options: The speed at A is the same as at C
It takes longer to travel from A to B than it does from B to C
The total time of flight is twice the time it takes to reach point B
The horizontal displacement from A to D is independent of the launch velocity

questions.question: The diagram shows a conical pendulum rotating with a constant speed. Which diagram represents the forces applied to the bob?
questions.answer: Only two forces act: tension along the string and weight. The centripetal force is their resultant, not an extra force.

questions.question: A light aluminium bar is placed on two horizontal metal rails connected to a power supply, as shown in the top view. The bar and rails are in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page, and the bar is free to move. What does the bar do when the switch is closed?
questions.answer: Current flows down the page through the bar. With the field into the page, the force on the bar is to the right.

questions.question: Sirius A has an absolute magnitude of 1.4 and is a spectral type A star. Which wavelength best approximates the peak wavelength at which Sirius A is emitting?
questions.answer: From the diagram a type A star has $T\approx10\,000$ K, so $\lambda_{max}=\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{10^4}=290$ nm.

questions.question: The rate of decay of a sample of magnesium-28 was measured over time (in hours). Which value is the decay constant of magnesium-28, in h⁻¹?
questions.answer: The half-life is about 20 h, so $\lambda=\dfrac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}}\approx3.5\times10^{-2}\ \text{h}^{-1}$.

questions.question: The emission spectrum from an unknown light source is shown with the spectra of some elements. What elements are present in the light source?
questions.answer: All the mercury, helium and sodium lines appear in the unknown spectrum.

questions.question: A train is accelerating uniformly to the left. A mass on a string makes a constant angle to the vertical as shown. The string breaks and the mass falls. Which diagram shows the trajectory of the mass as observed by a person sitting in the train?
questions.answer: In the train's frame the mass starts at rest and has a constant apparent acceleration (gravity plus the effect of the train's acceleration) along the original line of the string, so it moves in a straight line.

questions.question: A proton starts from rest at the positive plate and is accelerated through a potential difference of 1550 V between parallel plates 20.0 cm apart. What is its de Broglie wavelength when it reaches the bottom plate?
questions.answer: $v=\sqrt{2qV/m}=5.45\times10^5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}=7.27\times10^{-13}$ m.

questions.question: The graph shows how the current in a brushed motor varies after start-up. Which statement is true?
questions.answer: Back emf grows with speed, so the net emf and hence the current fall.
options: As the motor gains speed the momentum increases, reducing the input energy required
As the speed of the motor increases the back emf increases, which reduces the net emf
The current changes because the input voltage is changing to keep the speed constant
The resistance of the rotor increases as it heats up, which reduces the current in the first 0.5 s

questions.question: Light is shone onto two metals to investigate the photoelectric effect. Which statement is true about the two metals?
questions.answer: Metal 1 has the lower threshold frequency, so more frequencies can eject electrons from it.
options: Metal 1 has a greater work function than Metal 2
Metal 2 has a lower threshold frequency than Metal 1
For both metals a higher frequency will produce a greater current
Metal 1 will emit electrons over a greater range of light frequencies

questions.question: A magnet is dropped through a solenoid and the emf generated is recorded by a data logger. Which graph shows the result of this experiment?
questions.answer: The emf reverses sign as the magnet leaves the coil, and because the magnet is moving faster then, the second peak is taller and narrower.

questions.question: The diagrams show apparatus used to explore different aspects of the atom. Which option correctly links the scientist to the apparatus they used (apparatus 1, 2, 3)?
questions.answer: Apparatus 1 is Thomson's charge-to-mass ratio tube, 2 is Rutherford's (Geiger–Marsden) alpha scattering and 3 is Millikan's oil drop.

questions.question: The diagram shows water waves passing through two openings in a barrier. Which two aspects of wave behaviour best explain the pattern on the right-hand side of the barrier?
questions.answer: The waves diffract at each opening and the two sets of waves interfere.

questions.question:
| Planet | Orbital period (Earth years) | Average distance from Sun (km) | Diameter (km) | Mass (kg) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Neptune | 165 | $4.48\times10^{9}$ | 49 200 | $1.02\times10^{26}$ |
| Pluto | 248 | $5.91\times10^{9}$ | 2380 | $1.31\times10^{22}$ |

Show that the information in the table is consistent with Kepler's third law.
questions.answer:
Kepler's third law: $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}=\dfrac{GM}{4\pi^2}$ is the same for all bodies orbiting the Sun.

Neptune: $\dfrac{(4.48\times10^9)^3}{165^2}=3.30\times10^{24}$. Pluto: $\dfrac{(5.91\times10^9)^3}{248^2}=3.36\times10^{24}$ (km³ yr⁻²).

The two values agree to within about 2%, so the data are consistent with the law.

questions.question:
| Planet | Orbital period (Earth years) | Average distance from Sun (km) | Diameter (km) | Mass (kg) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Neptune | 165 | $4.48\times10^{9}$ | 49 200 | $1.02\times10^{26}$ |
| Pluto | 248 | $5.91\times10^{9}$ | 2380 | $1.31\times10^{22}$ |

Calculate the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of Neptune.
Pluto has an elliptical orbit with an eccentricity of 0.244, as shown. Compare the orbital velocity and gravitational potential energy of Pluto at perihelion and at aphelion.
questions.answer:
Gravitational potential energy is $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. At **perihelion** $r$ is smallest, so $U$ is at its minimum (most negative); at **aphelion** $r$ is largest, so $U$ is at its maximum (least negative).

Total mechanical energy is conserved, so kinetic energy is greatest where $U$ is least. Hence Pluto moves **fastest at perihelion** and **slowest at aphelion**, consistent with Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times).

questions.question: Derive the escape velocity equation $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}$, including specific reference to the relevant physical principle.
questions.answer:
The principle is **conservation of energy**: an object that just escapes reaches an infinite distance with zero speed, where both its kinetic and potential energy are zero.

Total energy at launch must therefore be zero:

$$\frac12mv^2+\left(-\frac{GMm}{r}\right)=0\ \Rightarrow\ v^2=\frac{2GM}{r}\ \Rightarrow\ v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}$$

where $M$ is the mass of the planet and $r$ the starting distance from its centre.

questions.question: A crane uses an electromagnet to lift a 2000 kg crushed car to a height of 11.5 m and then moves it sideways at $5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. When the car is directly above point X, the power is suddenly cut and the car falls to the ground. How long does the car take to reach the ground?
questions.answer: Vertically $u_y=0$: $11.5=\tfrac12(9.8)t^2$, so $t=1.53$ s.

questions.question: A crane uses an electromagnet to lift a 2000 kg crushed car to a height of 11.5 m and then moves it sideways at $5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. When the car is directly above point X, the power is suddenly cut and the car falls to the ground. How far from point X does the car hit the ground?

A crane uses an electromagnet to lift a 2000 kg crushed car to a height of 11.5 m and then moves it sideways at $5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. When the car is directly above point X, the power is suddenly cut and the car falls to the ground. What is the velocity of the car upon impact?
questions.answer:
$v_y=9.8\times1.53=15.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ down and $v_x=5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

$$v=\sqrt{5.0^2+15.0^2}=15.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$

at $\tan^{-1}(15.0/5.0)=72^\circ$ below the horizontal (18° from the vertical), in the direction the car was moving.

questions.question: Explain why the presence of a bank on a curve allows a racing car to travel faster than on a horizontal curve of the same radius.
questions.answer:
To follow a curve, the car needs a net force towards the centre of $F_c=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

On a horizontal curve this force is supplied only by friction between the tyres and road, which has a maximum value and so limits the speed.

On a banked curve the normal force is tilted towards the centre, so its horizontal component $N\sin\theta$ also contributes to the centripetal force, in addition to the horizontal component of friction. A larger total centripetal force is available, so for the same radius the car can travel faster.

questions.question: A step-up transformer is constructed using a laminated iron core, with coils made of copper wires of different thicknesses, as shown. Explain why the supply is AC not DC.
questions.answer: A voltage is induced in the secondary coil only when the magnetic flux through it changes. An AC supply produces a continually changing current in the primary and therefore a changing flux in the core, which induces a continuous (alternating) voltage in the secondary. A steady DC current gives a constant flux and so no induced voltage.

questions.question: A step-up transformer is constructed using a laminated iron core, with coils made of copper wires of different thicknesses, as shown. 20.0 V is applied to the primary coil. The input power is 15.0 W, the output current is 0.5 A and 14.0 W is dissipated by the resistor. Determine the voltage across the resistor and the efficiency of the transformer.
questions.answer:
$$V=\frac{P}{I}=\frac{14.0}{0.5}=28\ \text{V}$$

$$\text{Efficiency}=\frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}\times100=\frac{14.0}{15.0}\times100=93\%$$

questions.question: A step-up transformer has a turns ratio (primary : secondary) of 2:3. With 20.0 V applied to the primary, the voltage across the load resistor is 28 V. Explain why this differs from the voltage predicted by the turns ratio.
questions.answer: The ideal prediction is $V_s=20.0\times\dfrac32=30$ V. The measured voltage is lower because the transformer is not ideal: not all of the primary's flux passes through the secondary (flux leakage), and some voltage is lost across the resistance of the copper windings (with further energy losses from eddy currents and hysteresis in the core).

questions.question: A proton is projected into a uniform magnetic field and follows a semicircular path as shown. Explain the shape of the path.
questions.answer:
While in the field the proton experiences a force $F=qvB$ that is always perpendicular to its velocity (direction given by the right-hand rule). The force does no work, so the speed is constant, and since $v$, $q$ and $B$ are constant the force has constant magnitude.

A constant force always perpendicular to the velocity acts as a centripetal force, producing uniform circular motion with $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}$. The proton completes half a circle and then leaves the field, travelling in a straight line.

questions.question: A proton travelling at speed $v$ enters a uniform magnetic field and follows a semicircle of radius $R$, as shown. Another proton is projected along the same initial path at half the speed. Describe and draw the path of the second proton.
questions.answer: $R=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$, so halving the speed halves the radius. The second proton enters at the same point, curves the same way in a semicircle of radius $R/2$, and leaves the field travelling parallel to its original path, a distance $R$ from it.

questions.question: The proton–proton chain and the CNO cycle are processes that release energy in stars. What, besides energy, is the main product of both of these reactions?
questions.answer: Helium (helium-4 nuclei).

questions.question: In what type of stars do the proton–proton chain and the CNO cycle occur?
questions.answer: Main sequence stars.

questions.question: Outline one fusion process that occurs in stars other than the proton–proton chain and the CNO cycle.
questions.answer: The **triple alpha process** converts helium into carbon in the cores of post-main-sequence stars. Two helium-4 nuclei fuse to form unstable beryllium-8, which fuses with a third helium nucleus before it decays, producing carbon-12 and releasing energy.

questions.question:
A single rectangular loop can rotate inside a uniform magnetic field as shown. The torque is measured at different angles between the normal to the plane of the coil and the field.

| Angle (°) | 25 | 35 | 45 | 55 | 65 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Torque (N m) | 0.025 | 0.034 | 0.042 | 0.049 | 0.054 |

Plot a graph of torque against angle.
questions.answer: Plot angle on the horizontal axis and torque on the vertical axis with linear, labelled scales. The points lie on a smooth curve of the form $\tau=\tau_{max}\sin\theta$ with $\tau_{max}\approx0.059$ N m.

questions.question:
A single rectangular loop can rotate inside a uniform magnetic field as shown. The torque is measured at different angles between the normal to the plane of the coil and the field.

| Angle (°) | 25 | 35 | 45 | 55 | 65 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Torque (N m) | 0.025 | 0.034 | 0.042 | 0.049 | 0.054 |

A trend line appears to show that $\tau$ is directly proportional to the angle $\theta$. Assess the validity of drawing a straight line for this data.
questions.answer:
A straight line through the origin is **not valid**. Theory gives $\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$, which is not linear in $\theta$, and the data show this: the increase in torque per $10^\circ$ falls steadily (0.009, 0.008, 0.007, 0.005 N m) and $\tau/\theta$ is not constant. A straight line is only a rough approximation over a limited range and would give poor predictions outside it, especially towards $90^\circ$. A sine curve should be drawn (or $\tau$ plotted against $\sin\theta$).

*Note: the school's solution also accepts that a straight line is valid over this range; the data and theory show clear curvature, and the data do not support direct proportionality.*

questions.question:
A single rectangular loop can rotate inside a uniform magnetic field as shown. The torque is measured at different angles between the normal to the plane of the coil and the field.

| Angle (°) | 25 | 35 | 45 | 55 | 65 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Torque (N m) | 0.025 | 0.034 | 0.042 | 0.049 | 0.054 |

Predict the torque when the angle is $90^\circ$.
questions.answer: $\tau=\tau_{max}\sin\theta$ and, for example, $\tau_{max}=\dfrac{0.042}{\sin45^\circ}\approx0.059$, so at $90^\circ$ the torque is about $0.06$ N m.

questions.question: In a real motor the torque output needs to be uniform. Outline how one design feature of a real motor produces a much more uniform torque than a single rotating loop between flat magnet poles.
questions.answer: **Curved pole pieces** (with a soft iron core) produce a radial magnetic field, so the plane of the coil stays parallel to the field over most of each rotation and the torque remains close to its maximum, constant value. (Alternatively, several coils at different angles with a multi-segment commutator ensure a coil is always near the maximum-torque position.)

questions.question: A beam of unpolarised light passes through two polarising filters as shown. The plane of polarisation of the analyser is at $40^\circ$ to the polariser. The initial light, $I_0$, incident on the polariser is $3.47\times10^{-2}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. What is the intensity $I_2$ after it has passed through both filters?
questions.answer:
The first polariser halves the intensity: $I_1=1.735\times10^{-2}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. By Malus' law:

$$I_2=I_1\cos^240^\circ=1.02\times10^{-2}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$$

questions.question: What characteristic of the wave model of light is supported by the fact that light can be polarised?
questions.answer: Light is a transverse wave.

questions.question: The diagram shows two models of light from the late 1600s. Which of these models was proposed by Newton?
questions.answer: The particle (corpuscular) model.

questions.question: In the late 1600s Newton proposed a particle model of light and Huygens a wave model. With reference to general characteristics of scientific models, why was Newton's model eventually rejected in favour of Huygens' model?
questions.answer: A scientific model must explain observations and make testable predictions, and is rejected when it cannot. Young's double-slit experiment showed interference, which the wave model explains and the particle model cannot. Foucault later found that light travels more slowly in water than in air, as the wave model predicted and contrary to Newton's prediction.

questions.question: In the currently accepted model, light has a dual wave–particle nature. Why is this duality necessary? Provide examples to support your answer.
questions.answer:
Neither a pure wave model nor a pure particle model can explain all observations of light, so both descriptions are needed, each applying to different phenomena.

**Wave behaviour:** diffraction and the interference pattern in Young's double-slit experiment require waves that superpose; polarisation shows that light is a transverse wave.

**Particle behaviour:** in the photoelectric effect there is a threshold frequency, emission is immediate and the maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency rather than intensity. This is explained only if light arrives as photons of energy $E=hf$. Black body radiation curves are likewise explained only if energy is exchanged in quanta.

questions.question: When light is incident on a clean sodium surface, photoemission can occur. The work function of sodium is $3.7\times10^{-19}$ J. Monochromatic light of wavelength 651 nm is directed onto the sodium surface. Does photoemission occur? Support your answer with calculations.
questions.answer:
$$E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^8}{651\times10^{-9}}=3.05\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$$

This is less than the work function, so **no** photoemission occurs.

questions.question: When light is incident on a clean sodium surface, photoemission can occur. The work function of sodium is $3.7\times10^{-19}$ J. Light of wavelength 651 nm is directed onto the surface. The intensity of the light is then doubled. Explain how this affects the emission of electrons from the sodium surface.
questions.answer: Each electron absorbs a single photon, whose energy $E=hf$ depends only on frequency. Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons arriving per second but does not change the energy of each one. Since each photon ($3.05\times10^{-19}$ J) still has less energy than the work function, there is still no photoemission.

questions.question: The graph shows the black body radiation curves for two objects. Compare the temperatures of the two objects.
questions.answer:
By Wien's law $T=b/\lambda_{max}$. Reading the peaks as about 540 nm and 660 nm:

$T_1\approx5.4\times10^3$ K and $T_2\approx4.4\times10^3$ K.

Object 1 is about 1000 K hotter than Object 2.

questions.question: The graph shows the black body radiation curves for two objects. Compare the power output of the two objects.
questions.answer: The area under each curve represents the energy radiated per unit area, which is much larger for Object 1 because it is hotter (power per unit area $\propto T^4$). Assuming the objects are the same size, Object 1 has the greater power output, roughly $(5.4/4.4)^4\approx2$ times that of Object 2.

questions.question: The graph shows the black body radiation curves for two objects. If these objects were stars of the same size in our galaxy, and Object 1 was twice as far from Earth as Object 2, compare how bright they would appear.
questions.answer:
Apparent brightness follows $b=\dfrac{L}{4\pi d^2}$.

For equal radii, $\dfrac{L_1}{L_2}=\left(\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^4=\left(\dfrac{660}{540}\right)^4\approx2.2$.

$$\frac{b_1}{b_2}=\frac{L_1}{L_2}\left(\frac{d_2}{d_1}\right)^2=\frac{2.2}{4}\approx0.56$$

So Object 1 would appear only a little over half as bright as Object 2, despite being hotter and more luminous.

*Note: the school's solution stops without a comparison ("if the luminosity is known") and writes the ratio incorrectly; it is $b_1:b_2=\tfrac{L_1}{4}:L_2$. The assumption of equal size has been added to the question.*

questions.question: The diagram shows what can happen when a nucleus of uranium-235 captures a neutron. Uranium-235 has been used as a fuel both in atomic weapons and in nuclear power stations. With reference to the diagram and relevant physical principles, explain how uranium-235 can be used for both applications.
questions.answer:
**Fission.** As the diagram shows, a U-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, forming a highly unstable U-236 nucleus that splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing about three neutrons and gamma radiation.

**Energy release.** The total mass of the products is less than that of the original nucleus and neutron. The products have a higher binding energy per nucleon, and the mass defect appears as energy, $E=\Delta mc^2$, mainly as kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons and as gamma rays.

**Chain reaction.** The released neutrons can cause further fissions. A self-sustaining chain reaction needs at least a critical mass of fissile material, so that on average enough neutrons are captured rather than escaping.

**Weapons: uncontrolled reaction.** Highly enriched uranium is rapidly assembled into a supercritical mass. On average more than one neutron from each fission causes another fission, so the number of fissions grows exponentially in a tiny fraction of a second, releasing an enormous amount of energy as an explosion.

**Power stations: controlled reaction.** Low-enriched fuel rods are surrounded by a moderator (such as water or graphite) that slows neutrons so they are more readily captured by U-235. Control rods (boron or cadmium) absorb surplus neutrons so that on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes another. Energy is then released at a steady rate; a coolant carries away the heat to produce steam, which drives turbines connected to generators.

questions.question: The diagram shows some of the energy levels for a hydrogen atom. For an electron to move from $n=2$ to $n=5$, what energy photon would it need to absorb?

The diagram shows some of the energy levels for a hydrogen atom. How would absorption of the photon that moves an electron from $n=2$ to $n=5$ appear in the spectrum produced by passing white light through hydrogen gas?
questions.answer: As a dark absorption line in the continuous spectrum, at the wavelength of that photon ($\lambda=hc/\Delta E\approx436$ nm).

questions.question: How did de Broglie explain the presence of the different electron energy levels in a hydrogen atom?
questions.answer:
De Broglie proposed that electrons have a wave nature, with wavelength $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}$.

An electron can occupy an orbit only if its wave forms a standing wave around it, interfering constructively with itself. This requires a whole number of wavelengths in the circumference: $2\pi r=n\lambda$.

Each allowed value of $n$ therefore corresponds to a particular radius and a particular energy level; other orbits would suffer destructive interference.
